title: Bram and the Orchard
premise: Tamsin Eastwick has spent eleven years ghostwriting other people's love stories while refusing to deliver one sentence of her own — the confession she wrote to Bram Calloway, heir to the Eastwick orchard, and never sent. When a rival memoirist hires her and a misdelivered letter from her past surfaces in his papers, Tamsin returns to the orchard under false pretenses, posing as an archivist. There she finds Bram widowed, guarded, and quietly falling for the woman he thinks is a stranger, while the found family of orchard workers who once sheltered her begin to see through her. As the harvest deadline forces her hand, Tamsin must choose between protecting her professional secret and speaking the rehearsed sentence at last; she confesses everything during the cider pressing, loses Bram's trust, and wins it back by giving up the ghostwriting career that made her invisible — ending with the two of them planting a new tree where the unsent letter was buried.
about_author: Edmund Hartwell is the pen name of a former agricultural journalist who spent a decade documenting family farms across the West Country before turning to fiction. He writes about land, inheritance, and the stubborn arithmetic of the heart from a converted cider house.

chapters.title: The Unsent Sentence
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. In London, Tamsin finishes ghosting a celebrity's fake love story and privately rereads the decade-old letter she never mailed to Bram. Her editor dangles a lucrative memoir job with a rival author. Emotional beat: controlled loneliness; she insists the heart is trainable, containable — and almost believes it.

chapters.title: Postmark Eleven Years Gone
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. Sorting the rival's archives, she finds her own lost letter, postmarked eleven years ago, returned unopened — meaning Bram may have never known she existed beyond a summer fling. She accepts the memoir job as cover to travel to the orchard. Beat: shock curdling into compulsion.

chapters.title: The Archivist Arrives
chapters.summary: Bram's POV. Bram, widowed three years and drowning in estate debts, meets 'Ms. Vale,' the archivist hired to catalog the orchard's records. He notices she knows where the light falls best on the kitchen table. Beat: wary courtesy masking grief; first flicker of recognition he can't name.

chapters.title: What the Trees Remember
chapters.summary: Alternating POV. The orchard workers — Marta the forewoman, teenage Joe, ancient Ned — fold Tamsin into harvest routines, treating her as family without asking permission. She catalogs letters and finds evidence Bram's father intercepted her mail years ago. Beat: belonging arriving uninvited; guilt deepening.

chapters.title: Cider and Small Confessions
chapters.summary: Bram's POV. A storm traps Bram and Tamsin in the press house; they share cider and half-truths. He tells her about his wife; she tells him everything except her name and purpose. Beat: intimacy built on omission, tenderness with a fault line running through it.

chapters.title: The Rival's Deadline
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. The rival demands scandal material about the Calloway family for the memoir, revealing the job was always aimed at Bram. Tamsin stalls, fabricates, and realizes she's betraying both men. Meanwhile Joe finds her old photograph in the archive. Beat: rising dread; the mask slipping.

chapters.title: Intercepted
chapters.summary: Marta's POV. Marta, who remembers young Tamsin from eleven years ago, confronts her gently: she knew about the father's interference all along and stayed silent out of loyalty. Now she gives Tamsin until harvest's end to tell the truth herself. Beat: mercy as ultimatum; found family demanding honesty.

chapters.title: The Press House
chapters.summary: Bram's POV. Bram discovers the forged archival notes and the rival's contract in Tamsin's room, then finds the unsent letter among them. He reads the rehearsed sentence at last — alone. Beat: climax of betrayal; heartbreak sharpened by the realization he'd fallen for her twice.

chapters.title: Saying It Aloud
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. On the last day of harvest, before the whole gathered household, Tamsin publicly refuses the rival's money, exposes the memoir scheme, and says the sentence aloud to Bram — not the polished line from the letter, but a truer, stumbling version. Beat: catharsis; vulnerability without guarantee.

chapters.title: Where the Letter Was Buried
chapters.summary: Bram and Tamsin's alternating POV. Weeks later, forgiveness arrives slowly, through work rather than words. They plant a new apple sapling over the spot where the letter lay hidden, and Tamsin begins writing her own book under her own name. Beat: resolution; identity claimed, inheritance redefined as what we choose to keep.
